## Load Dataset

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
import re
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, split, explode, regexp_replace, transform, when
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.functions import monotonically_increasing_id

np.random.seed(42)
pio.renderers.default = "notebook"

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName("LightcastData") \
    .config("spark.ui.showConsoleProgress", "false") \
    .getOrCreate()

spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")

df = spark.read \
    .option("header", "true") \
    .option("inferSchema", "true") \
    .option("multiLine", "true") \
    .option("escape", "\"") \
    .csv("data/lightcast_data.csv")

df.createOrReplaceTempView("job_postings")

print("Rows:", df.count())
print("Columns:", len(df.columns))
```
This dataset contains job posting information that can be used to study salary trends, hiring patterns, and work arrangements. Before analysis, we inspected the number of rows and columns and reviewed the variable names to understand what cleaning would be needed.

## Drop Unnecessary Columns

We removed tracking fields and redundant classification variables where present so that the dataset is easier to interpret and use for analysis.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

columns_to_drop = [
    "ID", "URL", "ACTIVE_URLS", "DUPLICATES", "LAST_UPDATED_TIMESTAMP",
    "NAICS2", "NAICS3", "NAICS4", "NAICS5", "NAICS6",
    "SOC_2", "SOC_3", "SOC_5"
]

df_clean = df.drop(*[c for c in columns_to_drop if c in df.columns])

print("Columns before:", len(df.columns))
print("Columns after:", len(df_clean.columns))

```
We examined missing values to better understand data quality. Since our analysis focuses on salary, industry, and work arrangements, we kept only observations with usable values in key variables.

## Handle Missing Values
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_clean = df_clean.filter(
    (col("SALARY_FROM").isNotNull() | col("SALARY_TO").isNotNull()) &
    col("TITLE").isNotNull() &
    col("REMOTE_TYPE_NAME").isNotNull() &
    col("NAICS_2022_6_NAME").isNotNull() &
    col("STATE_NAME").isNotNull()
)

print("Rows after filtering:", df_clean.count())
```
We examined missing values to better understand data quality. Since our analysis focuses on salary, industry, and work arrangements, we kept only observations with usable values in key variables. This approach preserves meaningful observations while ensuring that key variables are available for analysis. This filtering step significantly reduced the dataset size, indicating that many job postings were missing key salary or classification information. While this reduces sample size, it improves the reliability of our analysis by focusing only on complete and usable observations.

## Convert Data Types

We converted posting dates to a date format so that date fields would be interpreted correctly.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_clean = df_clean.withColumn(
    "POSTED",
    F.to_date("POSTED", "M/d/yyyy")
)

df_clean.select("POSTED").show(5, truncate=False)
```

## Remove Duplicates
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

before_rows = df_clean.count()

df_clean = df_clean.dropDuplicates()

after_rows = df_clean.count()

print("Rows before removing duplicates:", before_rows)
print("Rows after removing duplicates:", after_rows)
print("Duplicates removed:", before_rows - after_rows)
```

Duplicate job postings can inflate counts and distort patterns. To prevent double counting, we removed duplicate rows. No duplicate rows were identified in the dataset after filtering, suggesting that each job posting is already uniquely represented

## Create Salary Measure

We created a midpoint salary using the lower and upper salary bounds to produce a single value for analysis. If only one salary bound was available, that value was used as an approximation so that we could retain more usable observations.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_clean = df_clean.withColumn("SALARY_FROM", col("SALARY_FROM").cast("double"))
df_clean = df_clean.withColumn("SALARY_TO", col("SALARY_TO").cast("double"))

df_clean = df_clean.withColumn(
    "salary_midpoint",
    when(
        col("SALARY_FROM").isNotNull() & col("SALARY_TO").isNotNull(),
        (col("SALARY_FROM") + col("SALARY_TO")) / 2
    ).when(
        col("SALARY_FROM").isNotNull(),
        col("SALARY_FROM")
    ).otherwise(
        col("SALARY_TO")
    )
)

df_clean = df_clean.filter(
    col("salary_midpoint").isNotNull() & (col("salary_midpoint") > 0)
)

df_clean.select("SALARY_FROM", "SALARY_TO", "salary_midpoint").show(5)
```
Instead of removing all observations with partial salary data, we constructed a salary midpoint using available values. If only one bound was present, that value was used as an approximation. This approach preserves more data while maintaining meaningful salary estimates. Job postings often report salary as a range rather than a single value. To standardize compensation for analysis, we created a salary midpoint using the average of the lower and upper bounds. If only one bound was available, that value was used as a proxy. This approach allows for consistent comparison across observations while preserving a larger sample size.

## Salary Summary Statistics

```{python}
#| echo: true

df_clean.describe("salary_midpoint").show()
df_clean.select("salary_midpoint").summary().show()
```
## Key Findings

The data cleaning process improved the usability of the dataset by removing redundant columns, handling missing values, converting date fields, and eliminating duplicate records. The exploratory analysis suggests that job postings are concentrated in a limited number of industries and that salary levels vary meaningfully across the sample. Remote and hybrid roles represent an important share of postings, which may influence how students approach their job search. The AI versus non-AI comparison is especially relevant to our project because it helps evaluate whether AI-related skills are associated with different compensation patterns.

## Visualization 1: Job Postings by Industry
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

industry_df = df_clean.groupBy("NAICS_2022_6_NAME").count()

top_industries = (
    industry_df
    .orderBy(col("count").desc())
    .limit(10)
    .toPandas()
    .sort_values("count", ascending=True)
)

fig = px.bar(
    top_industries,
    x="count",
    y="NAICS_2022_6_NAME",
    orientation="h",
    title="Top 10 Industries by Number of Job Postings",
    labels={
        "count": "Number of Job Postings",
        "NAICS_2022_6_NAME": "Industry"
    },
    color="count",
    color_continuous_scale="Blues"
)

fig.update_layout(
    title_x=0.5,
    xaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    yaxis_title="Industry",
    coloraxis_showscale=False,
    template="simple_white",
    height=550,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20)
)

fig.show()
```
A horizontal bar chart makes it easy to compare industries and quickly identify which sectors contribute the most job postings

## Visualization 2: Salary Distribution
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

salary_pdf = df_clean.select("salary_midpoint").toPandas()

fig = px.histogram(
    salary_pdf,
    x="salary_midpoint",
    nbins=40,
    title="Distribution of Salary Midpoints",
    labels={"salary_midpoint": "Salary Midpoint ($)"},
    color_discrete_sequence=["#4C78A8"]
)

fig.update_layout(
    title_x=0.5,
    xaxis_title="Salary Midpoint ($)",
    yaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    template="simple_white",
    bargap=0.05,
    height=500,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20)
)

fig.update_xaxes(tickprefix="$", separatethousands=True)

fig.show()
```
A histogram is useful for showing the overall shape of salary distribution and identifying clustering, spread, and outliers.

## Visualization 3: Remote vs. On-Site Jobs

## Visualization 4: AI vs. Non-AI Roles
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

df_clean = df_clean.withColumn(
    "ai_flag",
    when(
        col("TITLE").rlike("(?i)ai|artificial intelligence|machine learning|data scientist|deep learning|nlp"),
        "AI"
    ).otherwise("Non-AI")
)
```
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

ai_salary_pdf = (
    df_clean
    .groupBy("ai_flag")
    .agg(F.avg("salary_midpoint").alias("avg_salary"))
    .toPandas()
)

ai_salary_pdf["ai_flag"] = pd.Categorical(
    ai_salary_pdf["ai_flag"],
    categories=["Non-AI", "AI"],
    ordered=True
)

ai_salary_pdf = ai_salary_pdf.sort_values("ai_flag")

fig = px.bar(
    ai_salary_pdf,
    x="ai_flag",
    y="avg_salary",
    title="Average Salary Comparison: AI vs. Non-AI Roles",
    labels={
        "ai_flag": "Role Category",
        "avg_salary": "Average Salary ($)"
    },
    color="ai_flag",
    color_discrete_map={
        "AI": "#E45756",
        "Non-AI": "#4C78A8"
    },
    text="avg_salary"
)

fig.update_traces(
    texttemplate="$%{text:,.0f}",
    textposition="outside"
)

fig.update_layout(
    title_x=0.5,
    xaxis_title="Role Category",
    yaxis_title="Average Salary ($)",
    template="simple_white",
    showlegend=False,
    height=500,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20)
)

fig.update_yaxes(tickprefix="$", separatethousands=True)

fig.show()
```

## Visualization 5: AI vs Non-AI Salary by Industry
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

industry_ai_salary = (
    df_clean
    .groupBy("NAICS_2022_6_NAME", "ai_flag")
    .agg(F.avg("salary_midpoint").alias("avg_salary"),
         F.count("*").alias("count"))
)

# filter for reliability (avoid tiny samples)
industry_ai_salary = industry_ai_salary.filter(col("count") > 100)

pdf = industry_ai_salary.toPandas()

# keep top industries overall
top_industries = (
    pdf.groupby("NAICS_2022_6_NAME")["count"]
    .sum()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(8)
    .index
)

pdf = pdf[pdf["NAICS_2022_6_NAME"].isin(top_industries)]

fig = px.bar(
    pdf,
    x="NAICS_2022_6_NAME",
    y="avg_salary",
    color="ai_flag",
    barmode="group",
    title="AI vs Non-AI Salaries Across Top Industries",
    labels={
        "NAICS_2022_6_NAME": "Industry",
        "avg_salary": "Average Salary ($)",
        "ai_flag": "Role Type"
    },
    color_discrete_map={
        "AI": "#E45756",
        "Non-AI": "#4C78A8"
    }
)

fig.update_layout(
    title_x=0.5,
    template="simple_white",
    xaxis_tickangle=45,
    height=550
)

fig.update_yaxes(tickprefix="$", separatethousands=True)

fig.show()
```

A grouped bar chart was used to compare average salaries between AI and non-AI roles across industries. This format allows for direct side-by-side comparison within each industry, making differences in compensation easy to interpret.


## Visualization 6: Average Salary by Region: AI vs Non-AI Roles
```{python}
#Convert to pandas first
pdf = df_clean.select("STATE_NAME", "salary_midpoint", "ai_flag").toPandas()

#Group + average salary
region_salary = (
    pdf.groupby(["STATE_NAME", "ai_flag"])["salary_midpoint"]
    .mean()
    .reset_index()
)

#Optional: keep only top states by salary (cleaner chart)
top_states = (
    region_salary.groupby("STATE_NAME")["salary_midpoint"]
    .mean()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(10)
    .index
)

region_salary = region_salary[region_salary["STATE_NAME"].isin(top_states)]

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

regions = region_salary["STATE_NAME"].unique()
x = np.arange(len(regions))

# Convert to pandas first
pdf = df_clean.select("STATE_NAME", "salary_midpoint", "ai_flag").toPandas()

# Group + average salary
region_salary = (
    pdf.groupby(["STATE_NAME", "ai_flag"], as_index=False)["salary_midpoint"]
    .mean()
)

# Keep only top 10 states by overall average salary
top_states = (
    region_salary.groupby("STATE_NAME")["salary_midpoint"]
    .mean()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(10)
    .index
)

region_salary = region_salary[region_salary["STATE_NAME"].isin(top_states)]

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

pivot_df = (
    region_salary
    .pivot(index="STATE_NAME", columns="ai_flag", values="salary_midpoint")
    .fillna(0)
)

# sort states from highest to lowest overall average salary
pivot_df["overall_avg"] = pivot_df.mean(axis=1)
pivot_df = pivot_df.sort_values("overall_avg", ascending=False).drop(columns="overall_avg")

regions = pivot_df.index.tolist()
x = np.arange(len(regions))

ai_vals = pivot_df["AI"].values if "AI" in pivot_df.columns else np.zeros(len(regions))
non_ai_vals = pivot_df["Non-AI"].values if "Non-AI" in pivot_df.columns else np.zeros(len(regions))

width = 0.35

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.bar(x - width/2, non_ai_vals, width, label="Non-AI", alpha=0.85)
plt.bar(x + width/2, ai_vals, width, label="AI", alpha=0.85)

plt.xticks(x, regions, rotation=45, ha="right")
plt.ylabel("Average Salary ($)")
plt.title("Average Salary by Region: AI vs Non-AI Roles")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
